Preoperative comprehensive risk estimation for axillary lymph node metastasis in breast cancer: development and verification of a network-based prediction model

Baoqi Sun1,4, Guangdong Shao2,4, Mingming Shi2, Zenggang Sun3, Xiaolin Wang2, Yining Song2, Zheng Sun2, Zhanjie Jin2, Chunhong Xu2 & Guolou Li2

To prevent the overaggressive treatment of axillary lymph nodes (ALNs) in breast cancer, it is necessary to develop a convenient analysis method that accurately and comprehensively reflects whether ALNs are metastatic or nonmetastatic. We retrospectively analyzed data from patients who underwent surgery for breast cancer at the Weifang Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine between January 2019 and June 2023. Binary logistic regression analysis was used to predict the metastasis status of ALNs. The developmental data set included 531 patients (January 2019–June 2023). The validation set included separate data points (n = 178, January 2019–June 2023). Multivariate analysis revealed that positive findings on breast physical examination, ultrasound grades of ALNs, lymphovascular invasion, and Her-2 status had significant predictive value for metastatic ALNs. Based on these findings, a 5-grade risk scoring system and 3-level management recommendations were developed. The risk of metastasis ranged from 11.25 to 93.46%, which was positively correlated with an increase in risk grade. The areas under the curve of the development and validation sets were 0.895 and 0.865, respectively. Ultimately, a convenient, accurate and comprehensive web-based predictive model was constructed using various breast cancer clinical, imaging and pathological criteria to stratify ALNs according to the metastasis probability.

Breast cancer is a common malignant tumor that poses a significant threat to human health1. As the first station of breast lymphatic drainage, the axillary lymph node (ALN) plays a crucial role in breast cancer. Precise assessment and management of ALNs are of utmost importance for regional disease control, accurate staging of breast cancer, individualized treatment decision-making, and reliable prognosis evaluation1,2. Currently, sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) and axillary lymph node dissection (ALND) are clinically recognized as the gold standard procedures for assessing the pathological status of ALNs (pNx) in early-stage breast cancer2,3. However, both of these methods are invasive, and complications associated with axillary surgery, such as upper limb lymphedema, shoulder and back pain, arm numbness, and reduced arm strength, are inevitable, significantly impacting patients’ postoperative quality of life4,5. In recent years, the results of several rigorously designed prospective clinical trials, including the SOUND (NCT02167490), BOOG-2013-08 (NCT02271828), INSEMA (NCT02466737), and SOAPET (NCT04072653) trials, have been published. These trials investigated the feasibility of de-escalation surgical approaches for managing ALNs. Additionally, the KEYNOTE-522 study explored the efficacy and safety of novel neoadjuvant treatment regimens for patients with early-stage triplenegative breast cancer, with all reporting positive efficacy data6–10. In this context, current clinical practice demands a more rigorous and scientific approach for the preoperative assessment of ALN status in breast cancer patients, to enable the development of more personalized and precise treatment plans.

Currently, the most commonly used non-invasive methods for clinically assessing the status of of ALN include physical examination and ultrasonography. Compared to traditional physical examination, ultrasonography, with its high-resolution imaging technology, offers a more detailed visualization of the morphological characteristics of ALNs, such as size, shape, boundary clarity, and internal echo properties, thereby enhancing diagnostic accuracy. However, ultrasonography is limited to providing information on lymph node morphology and is subject to operator dependence and subjectivity, which can compromise its accuracy11,12. Although the application of ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) greatly makes up for the deficiencies of ultrasonographic diagnosis, the limited number of specimens obtained by fine-needle aspiration (FNA) may not fully reflect the extent of the disease, and the diagnosis is heavily reliant on the experience of the operator and pathologist, leading to a high degree of uncertainty13,14. To overcome the limitations of ultrasound diagnosis, multiple medical centers have developed a series of prediction models, such as the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC) model and SCH model based on breast tumor pathology features, as well as radiomics models based on PET-CT or breast MRI11,15–17. Although these predictive models largely mitigate the issues of operator dependence and subjectivity, they are characterized by incomplete coverage of predictive variables, high costs, procedural complexity, and limited popularizability, which restrict their clinical application12,18.

In practical clinical work, clinicians often need to comprehensively assess a variety of risk factors associated with lymph node metastasis when evaluating the status of ALNs in breast cancer patients. These include physical examination results, imaging features of the breast and ALNs (tumor size, tumor laterality, tumor location, diffuse distribution, multifocality, cluster calcification, etc.), pathological features of breast tumors (lymphovascular invasion (LVI), histologic grade, estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (Her-2) status, Ki-67 expression, etc.), and nonspecific systemic inflammatory markers (neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio (NLR) and platelet lymphocyte ratio (PLR), among others)15,19–22. Unfortunately, at present, we still lack a pragmatic and convenient model to comprehensively represent the overall significant features of ALNs. In view of this, this study intends to develop and verify such a web-based prediction model, thereby achieving hierarchical management of ALNs in breast cancer, fulfilling the purpose of precision medical treatment, and improving the patient’s quality of life.

Materials and methods This retrospective study was carried out in line with the moral standards stipulated in the Helsinki Declaration and the International Ethics Guide for Human Biomedical Research issued by the International Committee of Medical Scientific organizations. It was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Weifang Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine. The data collected in this study were all tested by Weifang Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine.

Study population Clinical data (sex, age, menstrual state, findings on breast physical examination, ultrasound grades of ALNs, tumor imaging size, tumor laterality, tumor location, diffuse distribution, multifocality, cluster calcification, histologic grade, ER, PR, Her-2 state, Ki-67, LVI, neutrophil count, lymphocyte count and platelet count) from 1022 patients with breast cancer treated in our hospital from January 2019 to June 2023 were collected. After excluding patients who did not meet the criteria for admission, 710 patients were ultimately enrolled.

The inclusion criteria were as follows: 1) Invasive breast cancer confirmed pathologically; 2) ALND or SLNB surgery having been performed; 3) Availability of histopathology and immunohistochemistry results for the surgical specimen; 4) Assessment of ALN status and breast masses by ultrasound and mammography within one week prior to biopsy; and 5) Completion of routine blood tests at our hospital with results available before biopsy.

The exclusion criteria were as follows: 1) Incomplete medical records; 2) patients who had undergone neoadjuvant therapy; 3) patients with bilateral or recurrent breast cancer; 4) patients undergoing palliative surgery; 5) patients with other types of malignant tumors; 6) patients with acute or chronic infections and hematological diseases; 7) patients with a history of axillary surgery; and 8) patients who were taking antibiotics, immunosuppressants, or hormone drugs before routine blood tests.

Breast physical exam All patients underwent a breast physical examination before the relevant auxiliary examination, and the positive breast signs included pathological nipple discharge, asymmetric thickening or nodularity, skin changes (peau d’orange, dimple sign, erythema, nipple excoriation, scaling, eczema, rupture), and secondary inverted nipples3.

Calculation of inflammatory indices Peripheral venous blood was taken from the upper limb on an empty stomach before biopsy and sent to the laboratory department of our hospital for determination by an automatic hematology analyzer. The neutrophil (N), lymphocyte (L) and platelet (P) counts in the blood results were recorded. NLR = N/L; PLR = P/L23,24.

Ultrasonic evaluation Two radiologists (with 15 and 10 years of experience in breast ultrasonography, respectively) performed ultrasound evaluation of the ALNs status and breast masses before biopsy. The image features of the ALNs status and masses were observed, measured and recorded. Tumor size was expressed as the longest diameter (cm) of the mass. Tumor laterality was recorded as left breast or right breast. Tumor location was recorded as upper outer quadrant, UOQ; lower outer quadrant, LOQ; upper inner quadrant, UIQ; lower inner quadrant, LIQ; central quadrant, CQ or multiple quadrant, MQ (the mass crosses two or more quadrants). The diffuse distribution of the mass was recorded as Yes or No. The multifocality of the mass was recorded as Yes or No. Multifocality was defined as foci of carcinoma separate from the primary tumor or a mass with diffuse distribution; no distinction was made between multifocality or multicentricity15.

The ultrasound grade of ALNs was divided into a negative group (including Types 1, 2, 3, and 4) and a positive group (including Types 5 and 6) based on cortical morphologic features. The cortical morphologic features of each type of lymph node were defined as follows: Type 1, hyperechoic with no visible cortex; Type 2, thin (< 3 mm) hypoechoic cortex; Type 3, hypoechoic cortex thicker than 3 mm; Type 4, generalized lobulated hypoechoic cortex; Type 5, focal hypoechoic cortical lobulation; and Type 6, totally hypoechoic node with no hilum25. When multiple types of lymph nodes were present in the same patient, the one with the highest grade was selected for inclusion.

Mammography evaluation The patients underwent mammography before breast biopsy, and each breast was routinely photographed in 2 positions, namely, the craniocaudal position and mediolateral oblique position. A double-blind analysis was conducted by two radiologists (with 5 and 10 years of experience in mammography, respectively) to analyze the mammography features. They reached consensus through consultation when different opinions were expressed. In this study, the image features of abnormal calcification in the breast were defined as 1) amorphous calcification of segment, line and cluster distribution; 2) rough heterogeneous calcification of single cluster distribution; and 3) fine pleomorphic calcification26.

Surgery procedure for ALNs The surgical methods for assessing ALNs include SLNB and ALND. For patients with clinically node-negative (cN0) status, ALNs were pathologically assessed using either SLNB alone or a combination of SLNB and ALND. For patients with clinically node-positive (cN1 +) status, ALNs were assessed using ALND. The sentinel lymph nodes (SLNs) were identified using blue dye and 99 m-Technetium sulfur colloid. In the protocol, an SLN was defined as any blue-stained node, any node with a blue-stained lymphatic channel leading directly to it, any node with a radioactive count at least 10% of the most radioactive node, or any pathologically palpable node. For patients with no more than two positive lymph nodes identified by SLNB, the decision to perform axillary dissection or not depended on the type of operation (breast-conserving therapy or mastectomy) and individual pathological characteristics 27.

Criteria for evaluating ALNs status The final status (metastatic or nonmetastatic) of ALNs was postoperatively examined using serial sections with hematoxylin & eosin (H&E) staining. Macrometastases (> 2 mm cancer foci) or micrometastases (0.2–2 mm cancer foci) of ALNs were considered metastatic. It should be noted that the isolated tumor cells (ITCs, < 0.2 mm) were considered negative in the final statistical analysis11,17.

Histopathological analysis Breast specimens were analysed by 2 pathologists with 20 and 15 years of experience in breast disease, respectively. The pathological features included LVI status, histologic grade, ER status, PR status, Her-2 status and Ki-67 expression. Construction of prediction model Of the 710 cases, there was only one male patient with breast cancer. This 1 case not only had no statistical significance in the total sample size of more than 700 cases, but also led to a decrease in the generalizability of the statistical results, so they were removed, and finally only 709 cases were included in the statistical data. Firstly, a random variable function was established for 709 cases of data included in the statistics. According to the quartile method, data less than 25% of the random number was defined as the validation set, and the remaining 75% of the data was defined as the development set. Then the stepwise regression method was used to screen out the variables with significant prediction efficiency from the development set, and the logical regression equation was obtained. The β value of each variable in the equation was the score of each variable, while the score of a variable that was not included in the equation was zero. The total score of each sample was calculated by summation. Next, the ROC curve was drawn using the verification set data to evaluate the prediction model. Finally, the prediction score of each sample was calculated by using the logical regression equation and arranged in the order from low to high. According to the order, the scores of all samples were equally divided into 5 segments, and each segment accounted for about 20%. The average metastatic probability of the sample in this segment was taken as the metastatic probability of the samples with this grade30.

Data and statistical analysis All statistical analyses were carried out using SAS9.4 international standard statistical programming software and the value of p < 0.05 was considered to be statistically significant. The enumeration data were described by frequency and percentage, the chi-square test was used for inter-group comparison; the median was used to describe the measurement data that did not meet the normal distribution, the t-test was used to determine whether there was any difference between the prediction results and the reference standard, and the nonparametric rank sum test was used for inter-group comparison. Risk factors were analyzed by binary logical regression analysis30.

Nine variables were entered into the MSKCC website (www.mskcc.org/nomograms): tumor type, LVI, tumor size, tumor location, age, multifocality, and ER and PR status. Subsequently, the probability of ALN metastasis was calculated for each patient. A ROC curve was drawn, and the area under the curve (AUC) was calculated. An AUC value between 0.5 and 0.7 indicates that the model has a certain accuracy, between 0.7 and 0.9 indicates that it has a good accuracy, and when it is above 0.9 that it has a very high accuracy31.

Results General characteristics of the study population Our study comprised 709 patients, 531 in the development set and 178 in the validation set. The descriptive characteristics of the development and validation sets are provided in Table 1. There was no significant difference between the development and validation sets. The rate of ALN metastasis in breast cancer patients was 51.22% (272/531) and 52.25% (93/178) within the development and validation sets, respectively. Based on the results of the univariate analysis, breast physical exam, tumor size on imaging, tumor location, abnormal calcification, ultrasound grades of ALNs, PR, Her-2 status, Ki-67 proliferative index, histological grade, LVI, NLR and PLR (p < 0.05) were significantly associated with the incidence of ALN metastasis. Multifocality was of borderline significance for predicting ALN metastasis (p = 0.0579).

Validation of the MSKCC model A comparison between the verification populations from the MSKCC and our patient cohort is shown in Table 2. The descriptive characteristics of these two populations differ with respect to surgery. The patients in our validation population included SLNB and ALND patients. Therefore, we verified the predictive power of MSKCC for ALN but not SLN metastasis. We could not use the MSKCC model to predict the likelihood that patients diagnosed with breast cancer with skin changes or diagnosed with ductal carcinoma in situ with microinvasion (< 0.1 cm) have positive ALNs. Therefore, we could not compare the subtypes between the two populations. Additionally, we excluded those patients when validating the usefulness of the MSKCC model. We input each variable data online to obtain the probability of MSKCC for each patient’s ALN metastasis and drew the ROC curve according to the real value and predicted value to assess the accuracy of the MSKCC model for predicting ALN metastasis in our cohort. As shown in Fig. 1a, the AUC value for the MSKCC model in our verification population was 0.817, and the 95% confidence interval (95% CI) was 0.784 to 0.851, which was significant (p < 0.001).

Establishment of the new prediction model We developed a new prediction model to overcome the limitations of the preoperative application of the MSKCC model. Establishment of the risk scoring system A 5-grade risk-scoring system was developed. Table 4 indicates the risk of ALN metastasis according to the clinical data characteristics of breast cancer. In this scoring system, the probability of metastasis was 11.25% in ALNs without significantly suspicious metastatic clinical data (grades 1). In other words, the false-negative rate of the scoring system is 11.25%. Additionally, the Spearman rank correlation analysis of the grading and metastasis risk of the scoring system showed that the rank correlation coefficient was 1, p < 0.0001. This showed that, on the whole, the metastasis probability increased with increasing risk grade, and there was a positive correlation between them. The reference standard was taken as the state variable, the total score was taken as the test variable, the ROC curve was drawn to verify the regression equation based on the ROC curve, and finally, the critical value of -0.06 was obtained (the risk of metastasis was considered to be high if it was greater than -0.06 points). The AUC value of the risk scoring system was 0.887, and the 95% CI was 0.862 to 0.912 (p < 0.001), which was statistically significant (Fig. 1c). This finding shows that the transition from the prediction model to the scoring system was stable.

Prospective use of the risk scoring system We randomly selected one-fourth of the total data as test data to internally validate the prediction model. As shown in Fig. 1d, the results showed that the scoring system performed well in the internal verification test (AUC: 0.865; [95% CI: 0.810 to 0.920]; p < 0.001). This finding shows that the model is suitable for use in routine clinical practice. Considering that the false-negative rate of SLNB averaged 8.4%, ranging from 0 to 29% across all trials. We divided the management recommendations on breast cancer patients’ ALNs into three levels according to the false-negative rate and the critical value of the risk scoring system: consider exempting SLNB (Grade 1, metastasis risk approximately11.25%), consider SLNB (Grade 2, metastasis risk approximately 34.4%), and consider ALND (Grades 3,4 and 5, metastasis risk approximately 74.17- 93.46%).

To overcome these drawbacks, we referred to the establishment method of the MSKCC model and developed a network based prediction model that combines physical exam, ultrasound grades of ALNs, Her-2 status and LVI (Tables 1 and 3). Generally, a model that performs with an AUC value of 0.7–0.8 is considered good, whereas values of 0.81–0.90 are considered excellent31. As shown in Fig. 1b, by analyzing the ROC curve of the prediction model, we obtained an AUC value of 0.895. This indicated that the prediction model we constructed in this study showed excellent predictability. Furthermore, when we selected the clinical data of another 178 patients to validate the prediction model internally, the results showed excellent prediction accuracy, and the AUC value of the internal validation set was 0.865 (Fig. 1d). The AUC values in these two populations were both greater than 0.754 of the original MSKCC model, indicating that our constructed model was more accurate15. Meanwhile, in comparison to prediction models developed by other research centers, such as the MSKCC model, the SCH model, etc., our proposed model was simpler to use since only four variables were included versus the nine variables in the MSKCC model and the five variables in the SCH model15,16,35. Although the prediction model in this study only includes four variables, these four variables come from three different prediction directions, making the prediction content more comprehensive. In addition, when we applied the MSKCC model to the retrospective data from our center to predict the probability of ALN metastasis, the AUC value was 0.817 (Fig. 1a and Table 2). Although this value is larger than the original MSKCC result of 0.754, it is still lower than the result of our prediction model of 0.895. We suspect that the reason for this result may be potentially related to skipping metastasis of ALNs. The analysis results not only provide indirect validation of the MSKCC model’s accuracy using external data, but also affirm the superiority of our prediction model.

According to an investigation report from the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO), the overall false-negative rate for SLNB was 8.4%, with a range of 0–29%36. Therefore, taking into account the potential risks and benefits of surgery, if surgeons are willing to accept a false-negative rate ranging from 0 to 29%, patients in the low-risk metastasis group may be considered for exemption from ALN surgery. Furthermore, to enhance the clinical practicability of the predictive model, we developed a risk scoring system with five grades. Each suspicious clinical characteristic related to ALNs metastasis was assigned a different risk score, and the risk of metastasis was determined by calculating the total score. As shown in Fig. 1c, the ROC curve analysis of the risk scoring system yielded an AUC value of 0.887, indicating that the transition from the prediction model to the scoring system was stable and reliable. After calculating the metastasis probabilities for different grades in the scoring system, we found that the ALN metastasis probability for grade 1 was 11.25%, which fell within the false-negative rate range of SLNB (Table 4). Therefore, in clinical practice, we suggest that exemption from ALN surgery can be considered for patients in the grade 1 category. Previously, several studies indicated that SLNB could be avoided when the MSKCC predictive value was ≤ 10%; however, the application of this criterion was limited due to the low proportion of patients who benefit from it within the overall SLNB population (7.7%)16,31.

Our study has some notable strengths and limitations. The strengths of this study can be summarized as follows. Comprehensiveness: The parameters of the prediction model encompass clinical examination, imaging, and histopathological findings, providing a comprehensive reflection of ALN status in breast cancer patients. Convenience: The model is freely accessible on the website, and clinical practitioners can easily input relevant prediction parameters to obtain automatic calculation of the prediction results. Intuitiveness: The risk stratification, probability of metastasis, and management recommendations for ALN metastasis are presented in a concise report format, making them clear and easily understandable. However, our research also has some limitations. First, this study is a single-center experimental study. The development set data and the validation set data were randomly selected from the total samples using the method of random function variables, ensuring no selection bias between them. To ensure the accuracy of the prediction model, the sample size of the development set was larger, specifically three times that of the validation set. Additionally, both the development set and validation set data originated from the same research center, meaning the validation set only served as internal validation. Therefore, we cannot ascertain whether these patients are representative of the general population. Fortunately, we included a larger sample size to mitigate any potential selection bias, and the risk scoring system we developed is freely available on our website, allowing researchers from other centers to use their data for external validation of our scoring system.Second, the potential for interobserver variability in the interpretation of pathological findings between the two pathologists was not assessed. However, given that the pathologists involved in this study had over 10 years of clinical experience in diagnosing breast cancer, the results may be more reproducible than if they had been evaluated by pathologists with less experience.

In conclusion, this study presents an accurate, comprehensive, and user-friendly multivariate prediction model along with an online risk calculator. This model will enable a true representation of the risk of ALN metastasis in breast cancer patients before surgery, thereby facilitating the selection of appropriate surgical protocols tailored to individual patients. It is worth noting that the universal applicability of this prediction model requires confirmation in future multicenter experimental studies with large cohorts that represent the general population. Until the prediction model is further evaluated, this predictive tool should be used with caution when deciding not to perform an ALN surgery in patients with a low risk of ALN metastasis.

## Abstract

Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) presents the most challenging subtype of the disease due to its aggressive nature and lack of targeted therapy options. To identify regulators of TNBC, we conducted a genome-wide CRISPR-knockout screen in both 3D tumor spheroid and 2D cell culture models. The 3D spheroid model displayed unique potential in identifying putative tumor suppressors due to its closer mimicry of in vivo tumor growth conditions. Notably, the chromatin-remodeling SWI/SNF complex emerged as a potent suppressor of tumor spheroid growth. Specifically, loss of the SWI/SNF ATPase subunit SMARCA4 promoted tumor spheroid growth with reduced compactness and enhanced primary tumor growth and metastasis across multiple TNBC models. SMARCA4 was required for the transcription of Rho GTPase activating factor ARHGAP29 by enhancing DNA accessibility through direct binding to its promoter. SMARCA4 loss resulted in reduced ARHGAP29 levels and hyperactive RHOA signaling, subsequently disrupting cell adhesion, facilitating the formation of a loose spheroid structure in vitro, and enhancing breast cancer growth and metastasis in vivo. These results establish SMARCA4 and SWI/SNF as tumor suppressors of TNBC through suppression of RHOA activity.

## Introduction

Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), which is characterized by the absence of overexpression of estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and human epidermal growth receptor (HER2), represents the most aggressive and hard-to-treat subtype of breast cancer. A deeper understanding of the novel regulators of TNBC tumorigenesis and progression through unbiased genetic or pharmacological screens is needed to identify new opportunities for therapeutic intervention. Traditional high throughput screens often rely on regular cell culture for their ease of handling and scalability. However, this artificial culture environment comprises limited aspects of the in vivo tumor characteristics. In contrast, 3D tumor spheroids or organoids, where cancer cells grow into spherical masses instead of a monolayer, offer more physiologically relevant models (1). The oxygen and metabolite gradients towards the core mimic the metabolic stresses encountered by native tumors. The organizing structure of spheroids further recapitulates physiological cell morphology, adhesion and extracellular matrix composition (2). Leveraging these advantages has led to numerous advancements in tumor biology and drug discoveries through 3D models (1,3–5).

The SWI/SNF complex is an ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler. It hydrolyzes ATPs to reposition nucleosomes and alter DNA accessibility. Through directly regulating DNA accessibility and engagement with transcription factors and other chromatin remodelers, SWI/SNF participates in transcriptional regulation and DNA damage repair. SWI/SNF complexes are highly diverse, with each individual complex assembled from a 29-gene pool comprising 10 to 13 subunits (6). Each composition may determine a particular DNA binding pattern governing gene expression programs in the development of specific tissues (7,8). In the context of cancer, individual gene loss within complex has been found to drive certain types of cancers, such as SMARCB1 in rhabdoid tumors (9–11) and SMARCA4 in germinal center-derived Burkitt lymphomas (12). Recent next-generation sequencing analysis of clinical samples revealed a pronounced mutation frequency of the overall complex. In all cancer types, nearly 25% of samples harbor mutations in at least one subunit of the complex. In breast cancer, SWI/SNF is mutated in 13% of tumor samples (6,13). The extensive mutation pattern underscores the potential broad involvement of the SWI/SNF complex in cancer progression. However, there is still limited understanding of the underlying mechanism the complex plays in regulating tumorigenesis and progression of breast cancer.

RhoA, a member of Rho GTPases, functions in various cellular processes with a pivotal role in regulating cytoskeleton organization. It is frequently overexpressed in various tumor types (14). In breast cancer, inhibition of the RhoA pathway suppressed invasiveness and metastasis in animal models (15–17). RhoA hyperactivation has also been shown to disrupt cell adhesion, a critical step for cancer metastasis (18–20).

In this study, we conducted a genome-wide pooled CRISPR-knockout screen using the 3D TNBC tumor spheroid model and identified a critical role of the SWI/SNF complex in inhibiting spheroid growth. SMARCA4, one of the two mutually exclusive ATPase subunits of the complex, exhibited a potent suppressive effect on tumor growth and metastasis. Mechanistic studies further revealed that SMARCA4 exerts its tumor suppressive function by inhibiting RHOA through transcriptional activation of the RHO GTPase activating protein ARHGAP29.

### RNA-seq

For spheroid samples, 100K cells were seeded with a density of 10K/ml cells to 10 cm ultra-low attachment plates and cultured in spheroid media for 8–10 days before harvesting. ### ATAC-seq

Spheroid samples were used for ATAC-seq. 120K cells were seeded with a density of 12K/ml cells to 10 cm ultra-low attachment plates and cultured in spheroid media for 9 days. Spheroids were dissociated with Accumax (Sigma) to generate single cell suspension. Dead cells were removed with the dead cell removal kit (Miltenyi, 130–090-101) to achieve at least 85% of live cells assessed by flow cytometry. ATAC-seq library was prepared and sequenced at the Genomics Core Facility of Lewis-Sigler Institute at Princeton University. The library preparation was performed on dissociated cells following the Omni-ATAC method (23). Briefly, 50K to 100K cells per sample were used as input to isolate nuclei, with 3 minutes cell lysis time on ice. The transposition reaction on the permeabilized nuclei was carried out with the TDE1 transposase (Illumina) at 37°C for 60 minutes, and then purified by DNA Clean and Concentrator-5 kit (Zymo). Illumina sequencing adapters and barcodes were added to the transposed DNA fragments by PCR amplification. The ATAC-seq library pool was sequenced on Illumina NovaSeq 6000 S Prime flow cells as pair-end 65 nt reads according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Raw sequencing reads were filtered by the NovaSeq control software and only the pass-filter reads were used for further analysis. Demultiplexed raw sequence file (FASTQ) were analyzed using Partek® Flow® software package. Specifically, raw reads were aligned to hg38-whole genome using Bowtie 2 (24) with -X 2000 and other parameters set as default, and duplicate reads were filtered. Reads from the non-targeting group (NTC) and the rescue group (KD2 + SMARCA4 OE) were merged. Peak calling was performed using the merged files with MACS 3.0 (25) with default settings. Bam files were converted to bedgraphs and normalized to CPM using bedtools. Bedgraphs were converted to tdf files and visualized with IGV (26). Each genotype of spheroid was sequenced once.

Agarose containing spheroids was centrifuged at 500 g for 5 min at 37°C to collect spheroids at the bottom. ### Western blot

Cells were washed with PBS and lysed in RIPA buffer supplemented with protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche, 11836153001) or protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (Thermo Fisher, A32961). Protein concentrations were determined by BCA protein Assay (Thermo Fisher, 23225). Samples were denatured by adding sample buffers and boiled. Routine SDS-PAGE and blotting were then performed. ### Gene-set enrichment analysis

For RNA-seq, GSEA (29) version 4.2.2 was used for pre-ranked analysis performed with log2 fold-change as rank list. Statistical significance was calculated by comparing the enrichment score to enrichment results generated from 1,000 random permutations. For CRISPR screen, genes with FDR < 0.25 were selected, and the top 200 positively or negatively selected genes were used for computing overlap.

### CRISPR screen pooled-knockout cell generation

SUM159 cell line was transduced with lentiviruses carrying pLenti-Cas9-Blast. A clonal Cas9-expressing cell line was selected (SCP7) with similar growth rate and morphology to the parental. Oligos of the Brunello library were synthesized and cloned into pLentiGuide-Puro in collaboration with Synbio Technologies. Next-generation sequencing was performed using the pooled gRNA plasmids to ensure library quality and even gRNA distribution. Viral supernatant was harvested at 48 and 72 hours post transfection, filtered through a 0.45 μm low protein-binding membrane (Millipore), and concentrated with Optima™ XE-100 ultracentrifuge for 2 hours at 4°C at 20,000 rpm. Virus pellets were resuspended with PBS to achieve a concentration of 100x, prior to aliquoting and freezing at −80°C. SUM159-SCP7 was then transduced with the library in three independent infection replicates, with >1000x library representation (cells per gRNA) in each replicate. Transduced cells were selected with puromycin 48 h post releasing the infection, and survived cells were counted. The probability (P) of a cell being infected by n viral particles, given an multiplicity of infection (MOI) of m, follows the Poisson distribution where P(n) = (mn · e−m) / n!. Appropriate MOI was determined by 20%–40% of cells survived after puromycin, which corresponds to an MOI of 0.2–0.5 and a single-infection percentage of 77% (at 40% survival) to 89% (at 20% survival). After puromycin selection, cells were cultured in 2D for an additional five days to allow for completion of gene knockout (designated as Day 0) before seeding to either 2D or 3D for the screen. During culturing, 2D cells were passaged every three days and 3D spheroids underwent media change every three days.

### CRISPR screen data analysis

Genomic DNA from 2D and 3D cultures was extracted using QIAamp Blood Midi Kit (QIAGEN) at Day 1 (~16hr after initial seeding to 2D or 3D) and Day 10 of culturing. The gRNA library representation was determined using a two-step PCR process in which PCR1 amplifies the lentiviral sequence containing the 20 bp gRNA cassette and PCR2 attaches Illumina sequencing adapters and barcodes. Primer sequences were obtained and modified from the Zhang lab online resource (http://genome-engineering.org/gecko/). All PCR reactions were performed using Herculase II Fusion DNA Polymerase (Agilent). Sufficient PCR1 reactions were performed to maintain library coverage. A total of 200 μg of genomic DNA template was used per sample with 5 μg of gDNA per 100 μL PCR1 reaction, ≤40 PCR1 reactions occurred per biologic sample. After pooling the PCR1 product, 5 μL was used for each PCR2 reaction. PCR2 was performed with at least four PCR2 reactions per sample. The pooled PCR products of each sample were then gel purified from a 2% E-gel EX (Life Technologies) using the QIAGEN PCR purification kit, and quantified with dsDNA High-Sensitivity Qubit (Life Technologies) and Bioanalyzer. Different samples were combined and normalized to the same concentration using TE buffer and sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq 2000. Raw reads were demultiplexed and the adapters trimmed to leave only the 20 bp gRNA spacer sequences. Downstream analysis was performed through MAGeCK (RRID:SCR_025016) (30). gRNA counts were normalized and three replicates for each condition were pooled together. Maximum likelihood estimation mode was used for comparisons between different conditions.

### Statistical analysis

Unless otherwise specified, data are presented as mean ± SEM and p values were calculated with unpaired, Student’s t test with unequal variance assumption. All statistical tests are two-tailed.

## Results

### Pooled CRISPR-knockout screen in 3D tumor spheroids identified known and putative tumor suppressors

To identify novel tumor growth regulators in triple negative breast cancer (TNBC), we conducted a genome-wide pooled CRISPR-knockout screen in both 3D tumor spheroids and 2D conventional cultures using SUM159-SCP7, a single cell-derived clonal subline of the SUM159 human TNBC cell line (31) (Fig. 1A). Lentiviruses carrying the human genome CRISPR-knockout Brunello library were used to transduce SUM159-SCP7 cells and generate the knockout cell pool. With controlled multiplicity of infection, the majority (77%–89%) of cells incorporated a single-gene knockout. Cells were seeded to achieve a >1,000x coverage per gRNA in each of the three replicate experiments and cultured for 10 days in both 2D and 3D. High-throughput sequencing was used to measure the gRNA abundance on Day 1 and Day 10, and the data were processed with MAGeCK (30) to identify gene hits.

Beta scores derived from MAGeCK, indicating the magnitude of selection from specific gene knockouts, showed consistency between replicates (Supplementary Fig. S1A, Supplementary Table S2). Positive beta scores correspond to a beneficial role for cell growth after gene knockouts, indicative of putative tumor suppressors. Conversely, negative beta scores implied putative oncogenes. The screen result of 10-day 3D spheroids displayed significant variation from Day 1. This contrasts with 2D, which remained quite similar to the initial culture on Day 10 (Supplementary Fig. S1A). Furthermore, three replicates of 10-day 3D screen produced consistent enrichment of gRNAs. This indicates that the 3D spheroid model, which mimics key features of in vivo tumors with limited access to oxygen and nutrition in the core, as well as physiologically relevant intercellular and cell-matrix interactions, may represent a more appropriate model to screen for cancer-related genes that would not have been possible using the 2D cell culture model.

For genes with significant negative beta scores, both 2D and 3D identified an abundant number of hits (Fig. 1B). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) to gene ontology signatures revealed that the top negatively selected genes (putative oncogenes) in both 2D and 3D are associated with essential cell survival and proliferation processes such as chromosome organization, DNA replication and damage repair, transcription, translation, and ATP metabolism (Supplementary Fig. S1B). Remarkably, for genes with positive beta scores (putative tumor suppressors), there are profoundly more hits from the 10-day 3D screen compared to nearly no hits from the 2D screen (Fig. 1B). Among the top hits were well-established tumor suppressors including KEAP1 (ranked #1 in 3D screen), NF2 (#2), and PTEN (#3).

To assess the overall efficacy of 2D and 3D in identifying known tumor regulators, we compared the hits to the functionally validated tumor gene database from COSMIC (32). This revealed that while both 2D and 3D selected for known oncogenes, only 3D demonstrated selection power towards known tumor suppressors (Fig. 1C). This finding is consistent with a previous study using lung cancer spheroid models (33).

We also performed GSEA on gene ontology signatures for top positively selected genes (putative tumor suppressor). For 2D screen hits, no gene set was identified with FDR<0.05, suggesting little functional convergence in these 2D hits. In contrast, 3D screen identified a significant number of gene sets with FDR<0.05, with the top gene sets related to TOR signaling and the SWI/SNF complex (Fig. 1D, left panel). We were particularly interested in the selection of the SWI/SNF complex, an epigenetic regulator that is emerging as a key regulator in cancer. Among the top 10 gene sets, SWI/SNF subunits were present in the leading-edge genes for five gene sets (Fig. 1D, right panel). For all 29 SWI/SNF subunits, the majority exhibited an inhibitory effect on spheroid growth (beta score>0), with SMARCA4, DPF2, and SMARCB1 ranking within the top 20 3D positive hits (Fig. 1E). These results indicate that the complex plays a critical suppressive role for tumor spheroid growth.

### Knockdown of the SWI/SNF ATPase SMARCA4 increases tumor spheroid growth with reduced compactness

We focused on the most positively selected SWI/SNF gene, SMARCA4 (ranked #6 in all 3D positive hits), for subsequent investigations. SMARCA4 is one of the two ATPases necessary for the chromatin regulation function of the complex. We generated short hairpin RNA (shRNA)-mediated SMARCA4 knockdown (KD) cell lines using SUM159-SCP7 (Fig. 2A). Contrary to a previous report that showed significant reduction in the paralog ATPase SMARCA2 level after SMARCA4 knockout in 293T (34), we did not observe a significant change in SMARCA2 expression following SMARCA4 knockdown in SUM159-SCP7 (Supplementary Fig. S1C). We confirmed that shRNA-mediated SMARCA4 knockdown increased spheroid growth similar to the effect observed in pooled gRNA screen. SMACA4 knockdown cells display an increase in both spheroid volume and DNA amount (proportional to cell number), at 10 days after 3D culturing (Fig. 2B), and such increase is more dramatic in KD2 cells which has a more complete KD of SMARCA4 than KD1 cells. These increases were rescued by re-expressing SMARCA4 (Fig. 2A, B). The EdU assay showed a higher proportion of cells in the S phase, supporting increased cell proliferation (Fig. 2C, D). Notably, the volume increase was disproportionately larger than the DNA amount increase, suggesting a larger unit volume occupied by each cell. We calculated the volume-to-DNA ratio as a measurement of spheroid looseness and found a two-fold and six-fold increase for KD1 and KD2, respectively. The knockdown spheroids were less compact when examined under microscope (Supplementary Fig. S1D). Spheroid sectioning further showed signs of reduced compactness, with cells detached from the spheroid body during sample processing, and the absence of the layer of stretched cells lining the periphery seen in the none-targeting control (NTC) spheroids (Fig. 2E). Together, these results confirmed the initial screen result of increased spheroid growth with SMARCA4 loss, with additional findings of reduced spheroid compactness when SMARA4 is lost.

To investigate the role of SMARCA4 in non-TNBC cell lines, we generated SMARCA4 knockdown and overexpression in ER+HER2− (MCF7 and T47D) and ER−HER2+ (BT474) breast cancer cell lines. RT-qPCR confirmed successful SMARCA4 knockdown and overexpression in these cell lines (Supplementary Fig. S1E). Consistent with our results from the TNBC SUM159 SCP7 model, SMARCA4 OE inhibited spheroid growth in the ER−HER2+ BT474, although SMARCA4 KD did not alter the growth of BT474 cells due to the relatively low baseline expression level of SMARCA4 in these cells. On the contrary, SMARCA4 knockdown reduced spheroid size in ER+HER2− lines (MCF7, T47D) (Supplementary Fig. S1F). Previous studies found SMARCA4 contributes to ER-mediated transcriptional activity (35), which may explain the reduced spheroid growth observed upon SMARCA4 loss in ER+ lines, as these tumor cells reply on ER signaling for growth and proliferation. Additionally, both ER+ cell lines carry mutations in SWI/SNF complex genes (BICRA in MCF7 and ARID1A in T47D), while BT474 and SUM159 are wild type for all SWI/SNF subunits. The presence of mutations in SWI/SNF may alter the complex’s function, which could account for the lack of effect of SMARCA4 overexpression on spheroid growth in these two ER+ cell lines. Further investigation is warranted to elucidate the molecular basis for the subtype-specific effects of SMARCA4 on spheroid growth.

### SMARCA4 knockdown promotes primary tumor growth and metastasis in multiple triple-negative breast cancer cell models

To further investigate the tumor-suppressive function of SMARCA4 in vivo, we performed orthotopic xenografts by injecting SCP7 cells into the mammary fat pad (MFP) of NSG mice. Surprisingly, neither the parental nor the non-targeting control SCP7 cells showed tumorigenesis ability until Day 80 of monitoring, following injection of 100K cells. In contrast, SMARCA4 knockdown led to rapid onset of tumors, with 100% incidence observed within 40 days post-injection (Fig. 3A and B).

To assess the effect of SMARCA4 loss in other TNBC models, we generated SMARCA4 knockdown using the more effective KD2 shRNA in the MDA-MB-231 TNBC cell line (36) (Fig. 3C). Xenografts with MFP injection in NSG mice showed an increased primary tumor growth rate for SMARCA4 knockdown compared to control, with a trend of increased spontaneous lung metastasis in (Fig. 3D, E). Since SMARCA4 knockdown enhanced both primary tumor growth and spontaneous lung metastasis, we directly evaluated the effect of SMARCA4 loss on metastasis by using experimental metastasis models. Tumor cells were inoculated into mice by tail vein or left cardiac ventricle injection to generate lung and whole-body metastasis (mostly bone metastasis), thus circumventing the influence of primary tumor growth (Fig. 3F). Initial tests with SCP7 cells showed extremely poor metastatic ability, making it infeasible for quantification. However, for MDA-MB-231 cells, we observed a significant increase of lung metastasis (Supplementary Fig. S2A, B) and systemic metastasis (Fig. 3G-I). Using the MCF10DCIS model, a TNBC-like cell line with features of basal B subtype that was experimentally generated from the immortalized MCF10A human mammary epithelial cell line (37,38), we also observed increased experimental lung metastasis following SMARCA4 knockdown (Fig. 3C, J-L). We further generated SMARCA4 rescue cell lines for MDA-MB-231 and MCF10DCIS (Supplementary Fig. S2C) and observed a clear trend of reduced metastasis upon SMARCA4 rescue in the SMARCA4 knockdown cells (Supplementary Fig. S2D-G). These results showed that the loss of SMARCA4 promotes primary tumor growth and metastasis in multiple TNBC models.

### SMARCA4 loss induces hyper-activation of RHOA-ROCK pathway to enhance tumor spheroid growth

To investigate the molecular changes associated with enhanced tumor growth and metastasis after SMARCA4 knockdown, we conducted RNA-seq on SMARCA4 knockdown and control spheroids (Fig. 4A, Supplementary Table S3). GSEA on hallmark signatures revealed overlapping changes between the two knockdowns (Fig. 4B). Overall, KD2 exhibited more pronounced changes compared to KD1, consistent with its higher effectiveness in reducing SMARCA4 protein level (Fig. 2A). Positively enriched gene sets include MYC targets and E2F targets, indicating accelerated cell proliferation as we observed in the EdU assay (Fig. 2B-C). Interestingly, the same gene sets were slightly downregulated in 2D knockdown cells (Supplementary Fig. S3A, Supplementary Table S4). EdU assay and cell growth monitoring in 2D culture also revealed a slight decrease in proliferation for SMARCA4 knockdown cells compared to control (Supplementary Fig. S3B-D). These findings suggest that the growth-promoting effect of SMARCA4 loss in 3D spheroid is not merely a result of intrinsic cell growth ability. Rather, SMARCA4 loss may help tumor cells overcome some growth barriers that do not exist in 2D culture but are rate-limiting in the 3D spheroid and in vivo tumor models, such as access to oxygen and nutrients or restrictions caused by intercellular adhesions. The disparate impact on 2D and 3D growth resulting from the same genetic alteration underscores the importance of using physiological relevant models to screen for functionally important cancer genes.

Among negatively enriched signatures, we found downregulation of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and apical junction (Fig. 4B). A significant portion of the down-regulated leading-edge genes were extracellular matrix components (ECM) such as fibronectin (FN1), collagens, and lysyl oxidase (LOX). Adhesion molecules also constituted a substantial portion for both EMT and apical junction gene sets, including Integrin B3 (ITGB3), cadherins, VCAM1, and Thrombospondin 1 (THBS1). Actin cytoskeleton regulators including RAC2, CALD1, WIPF1, and PDLIM4 are also involved in both gene sets (Fig. 4C). The mesenchymal markers were largely downregulated in KD compared to control, Specifically, FN1, CDH2, ZEB1, and SNAI2 showed a decrease of more than two-fold and a p value less than 0.1 in KD2 (Supplementary Fig. S3E). FN1(Fibronectin) and CDH2 (N-Cadherin) further showed a significant decrease in protein levels (Supplementary Fig. S3F). Conversely, the epithelial marker CDH1 remained in the bottom 20% in terms of expression level among all genes in RNA-seq and the protein were undetectable in western blot for both control and SMARCA4 knockdown. In MCF10DCIS, we also observed significant downregulation of EMT (Supplementary Fig. S3G). Taking together, these results suggest that SMARCA4 knockdown allows tumor cells to undergo a non-canonical or partial mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (MET), involving the loss of expression of some mesenchymal genes without gaining expression of epithelial markers, leading to the loss of intercellular or cell-matrix adhesions to promote cell movement. This cellular state is reminiscent of the hybrid or partial EMT state previously known to be associated with increased plasticity and metastatic potential of tumor cells (39,40).

GSEA of the RNA-seq data revealed that SMARCA4 knockdown led to enrichment of gene sets associated with expression of a constitutively active form of RHOA (41) (Fig. 4D, Supplementary Fig. S3H). This suggests that SMARCA4 knockdown induced transcriptome changes resembling a hyperactive RHOA, which is a Rho GTPase that has been shown previously to be a major regulator of cell morphology and adhesion. Moreover, a subset of leading-edge genes downregulated in EMT and apical junction were also found among the downregulated genes in RHOA transformation (Fig. 4E, Supplementary Fig. S3I). This implies that RHOA activation may lead to the loss of cell adhesion and enhanced spheroid growth.

Upon activation, RHOA GTPase signals through downstream effectors including the Rho kinase (ROCK). ROCK phosphorylates myosin regulatory light chain 2 (MLC2) at Ser19, which is critical in initiating actomyosin contraction and often used as a marker for RHOA-ROCK activation. We found that p-MLC2 (Ser19) was indeed increased in SMARCA4-knockdown spheroids compared to controls (Fig. 4F), consistent with augmented RHOA activity. Importantly, treating the SMARCA4 knockdown spheroids with ROCK inhibitor Y27632 resulted in a reduction in the p-MLC2 level (Fig. 4F). Furthermore, ROCK inhibitor treatment significantly reversed the increase in spheroid volume and total cell number, along with re-establishing the compactness in the spheroid structure (Fig. 5A). The EdU assay also showed that ROCK inhibitor reverted the increase in the proportion of cells in the S phase induced by SMARCA4 knockdown (Fig. 5B).

Besides Y27632, other ROCK inhibitors such as RKI1447 and Azaindole 1 also demonstrated the same effect in reducing spheroid size with re-established compactness (Fig. 5C). Spheroid sectioning showed that the missing stretched cells surrounding the spheroid boundary in SMARCA4 knockdown were restored by Y27632 treatment (Fig. 5D). In the RNA-seq experiment, we identified candidate genes regulated by RHOA to induce downregulation of EMT or apical junction (Fig. 4E). Y27632 treatment partially restored the mRNA levels of these genes (Supplementary Fig. S3J), confirming their role as downstream effectors of the RHOA pathway. Together, these results support that RHOA-ROCK becomes hyperactivated upon SMARCA4 loss and induces cell adhesion loss and promotes spheroid growth.

SMARCA4 is highly mutated in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), affecting 10–37% of patients (42–45). We also tested the effect of ROCK inhibitors on spheroid growth of the A549 NSCLC cell line, which has intrinsic loss of SMARCA4 expression (Fig. 5E). The Y27632 treatment elicited an effect similar to what we observed in SCP7 breast cancer spheroids with SMARCA4 knockdown, leading to reduced volume and increased compactness (Fig. 5F). The treatment also decreased the phosphorylation of MLC2 (Fig. 5G). We further generated wild type SMARCA4-expressing A549 cells and observed increased ARHGAP29 expression, and reduced pMLC2 (Fig. 5H), suggesting the regulation of ARHGAP29 by SMARCA4 is also consistent between A549 and SUM159-SCP7. Together these suggest a shared hyperactive RHOA status that is responsible for the loss of compactness in SMARCA4-deficient spheroids across SCP7 and A549. Future studies should investigate whether similar regulatory mechanism is common among other SMARCA4 mutant cancers.

### SMARCA4 facilitates ARHGAP29 transcription by binding to and enhancing the accessibility of the promoter

To test whether the change in RHOA activity was a result of direct transcriptional regulation on RHOA and ROCKs, we checked their mRNA and protein levels. In our RNA-seq data, SMARCA4 knockdown showed a moderate 1.2-fold increase in ROCK1 mRNA (Fig. 6A). However, western blot revealed no significant increase in RHOA, ROCK1 and ROCK2 protein levels (Fig. 6B). Therefore, we shifted our attention to the analysis of the Rho-GTPase regulators. Rho has intrinsic GTPase activity and GTP hydrolysis leads to the transitioning from an active GTP-bound state to an inactive GDP-bound state. This switch is tightly regulated by three groups of proteins: the GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs), the guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs), and the guanine nucleotide dissociation inhibitors (GDIs). GAPs promote Rho GTPase activity, leading to less active Rho-GTP, whereas GEFs accelerate the replacement of GDP with GTP, increasing the level of active Rho-GTP. The less common GPIs prevent the dissociation of GDPs, with both activation and inhibition effects identified. We examined the spheroid mRNA level of 47 GAPs, 42 GEFs, and 3 GDIs reported to act on RHOA according to the Reactome database (46). Based on the observation that SMARCA4 knockdown results in hyper-active RHOA, we searched for GAPs with decreased levels and GEFs with increased levels in the knockdown compared to control. (Fig. 6C, Supplementary Table S5 to S7). Among these candidates, we found that ARHGAP29 showed the most significant changes, with a 50% and 90% decrease in mRNA levels from two SMARCA4-knockdown spheroids compared to control (Fig. 6C). This decrease was confirmed with additional spheroid and 2D mRNA samples (Fig. 6D) and in western blot analysis of protein lysates from spheroids (Fig. 6E).

SWI/SNF functions through DNA accessibility regulation. Therefore, we conducted transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (ATAC-seq) assay on spheroid samples. ATAC-seq identified peaks mostly falling into intergenic and introns, corresponding to distal enhancer regions. About 20% of peaks were within 1kb proximity of transcription start sites (TSSs), corresponding to promoters (Supplementary Fig. S4A, Supplementary Table S8). We selected the top 200 upregulated or downregulated gene promoters from the knockdown pair (KD vs. NTC) and rescue pair (KD+Vec vs. KD+SMARCA4) to assess overlap to gene ontology sets (Supplementary Fig. S4B and C). The top 20 gene sets showed that genes with increased accessibility upon SMARCA4 knockdown were enriched in cell motility pathways, while those with decreased accessibility were enriched in cell adhesion pathways. These findings align with RNA-seq data showing reduced adhesion-related gene signatures and the in vivo phenotype of increased metastasis. For ARHGAP29, two of its promoter regions were identified as peaks, and their accessibility reduced after SMARCA4 knockdown and restored after SMARCA4 ectopic re-expression (Fig. 6F, G). We also performed ChIP-qPCR to examine the direct binding of SMARCA4 to these regions. Primers were designed to amplify the center of Peak 1 from ATAC-seq, corresponding to the ARHGAP29 promoter. A region upstream of Peak 1 served as the negative control, while a previously reported SMARCA4 binding site in the BCL2 gene promoter was used as the positive control (47). Compared to IgG pulldown, SMARCA4 antibody enriched DNA in the positive control and the ARHGAP29 promoter, but not in the negative control (Fig. 6H). SWI/SNF has been found to function in antagonism with the polycomb repressive complex (PRC), which adds the transcription-inhibitory histone marker H3K27me3. The absence of SWI/SNF leads to accumulated PRC binding and subsequent addition of the histone marker H3K27me3 (48). To assess whether this occurs at the ARHGAP29 promoter, we pulled down H3K27me3 with H3 as control and amplified the center of Peak 1 (ARHGAP29 promoter). Indeed, we saw an enrichment of the inhibitory marker in the knockdown group compared to control (Fig. 6I). Since EZH1/2 are the methyltransferase in PRC2 complex, we tested two EZH1/2-specific inhibitors on their effects on 3D spheroid growth and ARHGAP29 transcription. As previously demonstrated (49,50), tazemetostat specifically inhibits EZH2 at 1 μM, while valemetostat selectively inhibits EZH1 at 0.1 μM and both EZH1 and EZH2 at 1 μM. Inhibitors were applied at the indicated concentrations during cell seeding, and spheroid growth was monitored over 10 days with total RNA collected to quantify gene expression on Day 10. Both inhibitors restored ARHGAP29 expression in SMARCA4 knockdown cells (Supplementary Fig. S4D), and partially reversed the growth-promoting effects of SMARCA4 knockdown (Supplementary Fig. S4E). Notably, the growth effects from the inhibitor treatments only emerged after Day 6, suggesting that the epigenetic remodeling by EZH1/2 inhibition requires prolonged exposure. Collectively, these results suggest that SMARCA4 directly binds to the ARHGAP29 promoter, and its loss leads to EZH1/2 mediated-epigenetic reprogramming of and reduced accessibility, thereby suppressing ARHGAP29 transcription.

To test the regulatory effect of ARHGAP29 levels on tumor growth, we ectopically expressed ARHGAP29 in SMARCA4-knockdown SCP7 cells (Fig. 7A). Ectopic expression of ARHGAP29 significantly reversed the increased spheroid growth with reduced compactness caused by SMARCA4 knockdown (Fig. 7A, B). Next, we tested the in vivo growth of various SCP7 cell lines with altered expression of SMARCA4 and ARHGAP29, ARHGAP29 expression prevented primary tumor growth induced by SMARCA4 knockdown until Day 40 of monitoring in NSG mice (Fig. 7C). These findings confirmed the essential role of ARHGAP29 as a downstream effector of SMARCA4 in the regulation of tumor growth.

In addition to SMARCA4, we also investigated another SWI/SNF hit from the screen, SMARCB1 (ranked #20 in all 3D positive hits, Fig. 1E). SMARCB1 is an essential component in all SWI/SNF complexes except for the non-canonical BAF (34). Similar to SMARCA4, knockdown of SMARCB1 in SCP7 cells resulted in increased spheroid growth with reduced compactness (Supplementary Fig. S5A-C), while slightly slowing down proliferation in 2D (Supplementary Fig. S5D). The levels of ARHGAP29 mRNA and protein both decreased with SMARCB1 knockdown (Supplementary Fig. S5A, E). When treated with Y27632, the increase in spheroid volume, total cell number, and volume to DNA ratio by SMARCB1 knockdown were significantly reversed (Supplementary Fig. S5B, C). Moreover, SMARCB1-KD promoted orthotopic xenograft tumor growth of SCP7 cells, similar to SMARCA4 knockdown (Supplementary Fig. S5F, G). In MCF10DCIS, SMARCB1 knockdown did not alter the primary tumor growth but caused a trend of increased spontaneous lung metastasis, possibly due to a weaker knockdown of SMARCB1 in this cell line (Supplementary Fig. S5H-K).

To assess the clinical relevance of our findings, we analyzed the PanCancer Genomic database (51) and found that tumors with SMARCA4 mutations are associated with lower ARHGAP29 mRNA levels. Furthermore, for all 29 SWI/SNF genes, we identified 9 additional genes whose mutation status was significantly associated with ARHGAP29 levels, with 8 showing mutations linked to lower ARHGAP29 levels. This suggests that the overall integrity of the SWI/SNF complex is essential for ARHGAP29 transcription. (Fig. 7D). In the KM-plotter dataset (52), higher mRNA level of RHOA is associated with worse distant metastasis-free survival in ER-negative breast cancer patients (Fig. 7E), indicating its role in promoting metastasis.

## Discussion

In this study, we used genome-wide CRISPR screening to identify multiple SWI/SNF components that exhibit the growth-inhibitory function on TNBC tumor spheroid growth. Specifically, the ATPase subunit SMARCA4 plays a critical role in cell adhesion. Loss of SMARCA4 disrupts cell adhesion, facilitating oxygen and nutrient access and promotes spheroid growth. In mouse models, SMARCA4 loss promotes primary tumor growth and metastasis across multiple TNBC cell lines. Mechanistically, SMARCA4 directly binds to ARHGAP29 promoter. Loss of SMARCA4 resulted in the accumulation of H3K27me3 and reduced accessibility on ARHGAP29 promoter, decreasing its transcription. The diminished ARHGAP29 level led to hyperactivation of RHOA and subsequent loss in cell adhesion. Restoring ARHGAP29 levels reversed the tumor-promoting effects from SMARCA4 knockdown (Fig. 7F). Collectively, our study underscores the instrumental role of 3D models in deciphering the mechanism of tumor regulators and provides new insights into the putative mechanisms governing the tumor-suppressive role of the SWI/SNF complex in TNBC.

Previous studies found that SMARCA4 and the SWI/SNF complex are involved in multiple steps of DNA repair (53–56). While impaired DNA damage repair has been proposed as a potential mechanism underlying SWI/SNF’s tumor suppressor function, this hypothesis is not supported by the clinical observation of low mutation burdens in SWI/SNF loss-driven cancers (57). We used the Alkaline Comet Assay to assess the level of DNA breaks and found no significant increase in SMARCA4 knockdowns compared to control. Moreover, the ability of ARHGAP29 overexpression to rescue the SMARCA4 knockdown phenotypes (Fig. 7A-C) suggests that the changes induced by SMARCA4 loss are reversible, and not likely the result of irreversible DNA damage accumulation.

Few studies have reported the regulatory role of SWI/SNF on the RHOA-ROCK pathway. One such study (58) found that re-expressing SMARCA4 in a SMARCA4-null adrenal gland epithelial cell line SW13 increased ROCK1 expression and stress fiber formation, indicating a positive correlation between SMARCA4 level and RHOA pathway activity–contrary to our findings. On the other hand, a group reported (59) that rescuing SMARCB1 expression strongly inhibited RHOA activation, disrupted the stress fiber network, and dramatically decreased the invasion ability in SMARCB1-null rhabdoid cell lines. These findings from the two papers suggest a contrasting role of SMARCB1 and SMARCA4 in regulating the RHOA pathway. In breast cancer, a study (60) showed that SMARCB1 knockdown in ER-positive breast cancer cell line MCF7 upregulated RHOA, disrupted cell-cell adhesion, increased cell size, and enhanced cell migration. Our findings on SMARCA4-RHOA regulation align with the two reported SMARCB1-RHOA regulations, which indicate that the SWI/SNF complex is required for RHOA suppression and maintaining the cell adhesion integrity. Additionally, we identified the GAP factor ARHGAP29 as the mediator of SWI/SNF’s regulation on RHOA. It is worth noting that the involvement of RHOB/C as downstream effectors of ARHGAP29 cannot be excluded. ARHGAP29 has been reported to exhibit GAP activity and negatively regulates both RHOA (61) and RHOC (62). We used p-MLC2 as a marker for RHOA activity, which can also be regulated in a similar manner by RHOB/C. Nevertheless, our RNA-seq data analysis suggests that the transcriptome following SMARCA4 knockdown resembles that of hyperactive RHOA (Fig. 4D, Supplementary Fig. S3H), suggesting RHOA is the most likely candidate among RHOA/B/C.

We attributed the observed loss of compactness to cell adhesion disruption. However, further investigation is required to unveil the specific adhesion molecules being regulated and whether they contribute to the increased metastasis phenotype. Hyperactivated RhoA is known to disrupt cell adhesion in various cancer types (18–20), and is often mediated by the loss of inhibition from GAP (63). In endothelial cells, the ARHGAP29-Rho pathway is one of the key mechanisms that regulate endothelial junctions. Loss of ARHGAP29 induces RHOA-ROCK pathway activation, leading to stress fiber formation and contraction, as well as impairs integrin-based adhesion and adherens junctions (64–66). Rap1, a small GTPase has been identified as an upstream regulator of ARHGAP29 in endothelial cells, where it modulates local RHOA activity by translocating ARHGAP29 to the cell membrane. Disrupted endothelial barriers and vascular leakage are associated with diseases such as chronic inflammation and atherosclerosis. Although less well-studied in cancer, similar mechanisms may be utilized by tumor cells, with ARHGAP29 modulation serving to regulate adhesion, promote invasion, and facilitate metastasis. Further mechanistic studies in this direction are warranted to better understand this process and its implications for cancer progression.

SMARCA4 is a bona fide tumor suppressor for breast cancer in mouse models. Its single gene heterozygous knockout mice developed tumors with 9.2% penetrance and a median latency of 14 months, and predominantly 92% being breast tumors (67). In the context of human malignancies, the loss of SMARCA4 is characteristic to a rare type of ovarian cancer known as SCCOHT (small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type). SMARCA4 is the only recurrently mutated gene in this cancer type, with 75–100% patients harboring inactivating mutations (68,69). In human breast cancer patients, SMARCA4 is mutated in 1.8% all subtypes and 2.3% in the basal subtype (13), with even higher proportion of breast cancer exhibiting reduced expression of SMARCA4. Previous studies have demonstrated that SMARCA4 exhibits both tumor-suppressive and tumor-promoting activities in TNBC, the latter being closely associated with TGF-β signaling. Mehta et al. showed that SMARCA4, in the absence of the SWI/SNF complex, forms a novel complex with SOX4 to maintain chromatin accessibility at TGFBR2 regulatory regions. The resulting upregulation of TGFBR2 expression further amplifies PI3K/Akt signaling, contributing to tumor progression (70). Zhou et al. demonstrated that SMARCA4 and SWI/SNF complex is required for the expression of tumor-promoting genes TGFB2 and SOX2, whereas lncRNA TGFB2-AS1 binds SMARCA4 and suppresses this process (71). Conversely, SMARCA4 has been implicated in tumor suppression, including one study showed that loss of SMARCA4 lead to cisplatin resistance by activating YAP1-mediated EMT (72). The clear tumorigenesis effect in SMARCA4 knockout mouse model and our findings in TNBC support the tumor suppressing role of SMARCA4 in breast tissue. We focused on tumor-intrinsic effects in this study, with in vivo experiments performed in immune-deficient mouse models. Notably, the inactivation of the PBAF subtype of the SWI/SNF complex, which includes the SMARAC4 subunit, has been show to sensitize melanoma cells to T cell killing (73). This indicates potential conflicting roles of SMARCA4 loss, promoting tumorigenesis through intrinsic mechanism while enhancing immune surveillance by facilitating killing by T cells. An interesting future direction is to test how SMARCA4 status in tumor cells influences their interactions with the immune system in breast cancer.

The fact that multiple SWI/SNF components were selected as positive hits in the screen suggests that the loss of different components may converge on the same molecular pathway in promoting tumors. Indeed, knockdown of both SMARCA4 and SMARCB1 led to increased spheroid growth with reduced compactness in SCP7 and resulted in primary tumor growth in xenografts. This phenomenon can be explained if the absence of any of these subunits lead to the loss of function of the original complex. Under this assumption, the scope of affected patients with this common molecular change is the total patients with any one of the SWI/SNF components, rather than a single component. It is worthy to follow up on the other SWI/SNF hits in the screen and confirm whether they exhibit shared in vitro and in vivo phenotypes.

Most anti-cancer drug development focuses on inhibition of oncogenes, while therapeutic invention based on tumor suppressors are less common because the tumor suppressor proteins are no longer present to be targeted. One possibility for developing therapeutics against SMARCA4-deficient tumor is through targeting the genetic vulnerabilities of dependencies of these tumors, as was recently achieved by targeting DCAF5 in SMARCB1-mutant cancers (11). Given the essential role of hyperactivated RHOA-ROCK pathway in mediating the pathogenic effect of SMARCA4 loss in breast cancer growth and metastasis, targeting RHOA-ROCK presents as an alternative approach for the treatment of SMARCA4-deficient tumors. ROCK inhibition has been an attractive approach for cancer treatment given its involvement in almost all steps in cancer progression. However, systemic administration of ROCK inhibitors causes life-threatening hypotension resulting from smooth muscle relaxation, and local use through inhalation has emerged as an appealing alternative method (74). Inhalation can target both primary lung cancers and lung metastasis. One future experiment could involve assessing the effectiveness of ROCK inhibitor inhalation in inhibiting primary tumor growth in the lungs of SMARCA4-null A549 cells, or lung metastasis grown from TNBC cell lines MDA-MB-231 and MCF10DCIS with SMARCA4 knockdown. This will help to answer whether ROCK inhibitors can be a potential therapeutic option for SMARCA4-deficient tumors.
